Network Problems: Paths, Trees and Flows

Feeding 100 Million People a Year

  • The UN World Food Programme (WFP) assists about 100 million people in more than 80 countries a year
  • Its tool Optimus plans the food basket and its route together

The result

Iraq: 12% lower cost at the same nutrition (Peters et al., 2021). WFP’s planning tools saved more than USD 150 million (Peters et al., 2022).

Group 8 presented this application in Presentation 1. Optimus is a mixed-integer program; at its core is a network flow (today’s topic) with nutrient constraints on the basket, the diet problem. Both numbers are from the two papers’ abstracts (Crossref, 2026-11-06).

Seervada Park: Three Questions

Question Network problem
Shortest tram route from the entrance O to the scenic point T? Shortest path
Phone lines reaching every station, at least total length? Minimum spanning tree
Most tram trips per day from O to T, with a limit per road? Maximum flow

Distances in miles. Trams run from the park entrance O to the scenic point T; cars are not allowed in the park.

Network Vocabulary

Nodes, Links and Paths

Term Meaning
Node A point: a station
Link Joins two nodes, either way: a road
Arc A link with a direction, \({A \to B}\)
Path Distinct links joining two nodes
Cycle A path back to its start

The path O–A–B–D–T in red. O–A–B–O is a cycle.

Trees

  • Connected: a path joins every pair of nodes
  • Tree: connected, with no cycle
  • Spanning tree: a tree that reaches every node. With \({n}\) nodes it has \({n - 1}\) links

A spanning tree: 7 nodes, 6 links.

Supply, Demand and Capacity

Node Flow Here
Supply Out > in F1, F2
Demand In > out W1, W2
Transshipment In = out DC
  • DC: the distribution center
  • Capacity: the most an arc carries
  • Cost: per unit of flow on an arc

Shortest Path: The Solved-Nodes Algorithm

The Problem

Shortest path

In a connected network with a nonnegative length on each link, find the path of least total length from an origin to a destination.

  • Lengths can be miles, dollars or hours
  • Idea. Find the nodes in order of their distance from the origin: the nearest, the second nearest, and so on, until the destination
  • A node whose shortest distance is known is solved

Dijkstra (1959). The table form used here is the one the 2025 Exam 2 asked for, and the one the exam practice slides use.

The Solved-Nodes Algorithm

Iteration \({n}\) finds the \({n}\)th nearest node to the origin.

  1. Each solved node proposes its closest unsolved neighbor
  2. Total distance: the solved node’s distance plus that link
  3. The smallest total is the \({n}\)th nearest node: record its distance and its last connection
  4. Stop at the destination; read the path back through the last connections

Ties

Equal totals are solved together. Two last connections into a node mean two shortest paths.

Solved Nodes on Seervada Park

n Solved
node		 Closest
unsolved		 Total
distance		 nth
nearest		 Min.
distance		 Last
connection
1 O A 2 A 2 OA
2, 3 A B 2 + 2 = 4 B 4 AB
O C 4 C 4 OC
4 A D 2 + 7 = 9
B E 4 + 3 = 7 E 7 BE
C E 4 + 4 = 8
5 A D 2 + 7 = 9
B D 4 + 4 = 8 D 8 BD
E D 7 + 1 = 8 D 8 ED
6 D T 8 + 5 = 13 T 13 DT
E T 7 + 7 = 14

One click per iteration. n = 2, 3 is a tie: C at 4 directly from O, and B at 4 through A. At n = 5, D is reached at 8 from B and from E: two last connections, so two shortest paths. The red numbers above the nodes are the minimum distances.

Reading the Path Back

  • From T, follow the last connections: T ← D, and D has two, BD and ED
  • Through B: T ← D ← B ← A ← O
  • Through E: T ← D ← E ← B ← A ← O

Two shortest paths, 13 miles each

O–A–B–D–T: \({2 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 13}\)
O–A–B–E–D–T: \({2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 5 = 13}\)

The Shortest Path as an LP

Send one unit from O to T; each link is two arcs.

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{\textstyle\sum_{(i,j)} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{Oj} - \sum_j x_{jO} & \quad & {}= 1 \\ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} & \quad & {}= 0 && \qquad i = A, \dots, E \\ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{Tj} - \sum_j x_{jT} & \quad & {}= -1 \\ & x_{ij} & \quad & {}\ge 0 && \qquad \text{every arc} \end{alignat*} \]

  • Out minus in: 1 at the origin, −1 at the destination, 0 elsewhere
  • gurobipy: 13, with \({x = 1}\) on O→A, A→B, B→D, D→T

A preview of Part II

No constraint says \({x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}}\), yet the solver returns 0s and 1s: this is a minimum cost flow.

Three Kinds of Applications

Minimize the total Example
Distance traveled A tram or delivery route
Cost of a sequence of activities Replacing a machine: arc \({i \to j}\) buys in year \({i}\), sells in year \({j}\)
Time of a sequence of activities A flight route under the day’s winds

Nonnegative lengths

The solved-nodes algorithm needs every length \({\ge 0}\). The LP needs only that no cycle has negative length.

With lengths >= 0, a solved node’s distance can never fall later, which is why the algorithm may stop at the first time it solves a node.

Minimum Spanning Tree: The Greedy Rule

Connecting Every Station

Minimum spanning tree

Given the nodes and the length of each possible link, choose links so that a path joins every pair of nodes, at the least total length.

  • The answer is a spanning tree: a cycle would hold a link that can go
  • Seervada Park: phone lines along the roads to all 7 stations

The greedy rule (Prim, 1957)

Start at any node. Add the shortest link joining a connected node to an unconnected one; repeat until all are connected. Break ties either way.

The Greedy Rule on Seervada Park

Step Connected Links out,
shortest first		 Added Length
1 O OA 2, OC 4, OB 5 OA 2
2 OA AB 2, OC 4, OB 5, … AB 2
3 OAB BC 1, BE 3, BD 4, … BC 1
4 OABC BE 3, BD 4, CE 4, … BE 3
5 OABCE DE 1, BD 4, AD 7, … DE 1
6 OABCED DT 5, ET 7 DT 5
Total 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 5 14

Each step lists every link with one end connected and the other not, shortest first. The minimum is the only tree of length 14 (all spanning trees enumerated in the source’s header). Starting from another node gives the same tree here.

Why Greedy Works Here, and Where It Fails

Spanning tree: greedy is optimal

Split the nodes into connected and unconnected. Any spanning tree has a link across the split; swapping it for the shortest link across never makes the tree longer. So each greedy step stays inside some optimal tree.

Shortest path: greedy fails

Walk to the nearest new station each time: O–A–B–C–E–D–T, \({2 + 2 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 15}\) miles. The shortest path is 13.

  • The tree’s path from O to C is \({2 + 2 + 1 = 5}\); the road O–C is 4. A minimum spanning tree does not hold the shortest paths

The exchange argument is the cut property. The solved-nodes algorithm is also greedy, but in total distance from the origin, which is why it works: lengths are nonnegative, so a node solved now cannot be reached more cheaply later.

Where Spanning Trees Appear

  • Network design at least cost: telecommunication lines, power lines, pipelines, lightly used roads
  • Wiring in electrical equipment and data centers
  • Clustering. Build the minimum spanning tree on the distances between data points and delete its \({k - 1}\) longest links: \({k}\) clusters. This is single-linkage clustering

Two classic greedy rules

Prim (1957) grows one tree from a node. Kruskal (1956) adds the shortest remaining link anywhere, skipping links that close a cycle. Both find a minimum spanning tree.

Part II: Flows

How much can a network carry, and at what cost?

Maximum Flow: Augmenting Paths and Cuts

Seervada Park in Peak Season

  • Each road allows a limited number of tram trips per day, in the direction of its arrow
  • How many trips per day can travel from O to T?

A first try. 5 trips O→B→E→T, 1 trip O→B→C→E→T, 1 trip O→B→C→E→D→T: 7 trips. They fill E→T and E→D, so no route that starts O→C can reach T.

The Maximum Flow Problem

Maximum flow

All flow starts at the source and ends at the sink; every other node is a transshipment node; flow on an arc is at most its capacity. Maximize the flow from source to sink.

  • Goods through a distribution network, from factories to customers
  • Oil through pipelines, water through aqueducts
  • Vehicles through a road network

Several sources or sinks: add a super source with an arc to each source, and a super sink, and the problem is again a maximum flow.

Residual Capacity and Augmenting Paths

  • Residual capacity of \({i \to j}\): capacity minus flow. A flow on \({i \to j}\) also gives \({j \to i}\) residual capacity: sending it back cancels it
  • Augmenting path: source to sink, every arc with positive residual capacity

Augmenting paths (Ford and Fulkerson, 1956)

  1. Find an augmenting path. If there is none, the flow is optimal
  2. \({c^*}\) = the smallest residual capacity on the path
  3. Send \({c^*}\) along it: subtract \({c^*}\) from each arc’s residual capacity, add \({c^*}\) to each reverse arc’s. Return to step 1

Augmenting Paths on Seervada Park

Iteration Augmenting path Residual capacities c* Total flow
1 O→B→E→T min{7, 5, 6} 5 5
2 O→A→D→T min{5, 3, 9} 3 8
3 O→A→B→D→T min{2, 1, 4, 6} 1 9
4 O→B→D→T min{2, 3, 5} 2 11
5 O→C→E→D→T min{4, 4, 1, 3} 1 12
6 O→C→E→T min{3, 3, 1} 1 13
7 O→C→E→B→D→T min{2, 2, 5, 1, 2} 1 14

Labels are flow/capacity after the iteration; the red path is the one just used; the residual of i→j is capacity minus flow, and of j→i the flow. Iteration 7’s dashed red arc is B→E used backward: E→B has residual capacity 5 because B→E carries 5. These are the textbook’s seven paths; other choices reach 14 in another order.

Iteration 7 Sends Flow Backward

After 6 iterations, 13 trips:

  • From O, only O→A (1) and O→C (2) have room; A→B and A→D are full
  • From C, C→E (2); from E, both E→D and E→T are full
  • E→B has residual capacity 5: the 5 trips on B→E

Path O→C→E→B→D→T, \({c^* = \min\{2, 2, 5, 1, 2\} = 1}\): total 14.

What the reverse arc does

B→E falls from 5 to 4. In effect one trip moves from O→B→E→T to O→B→D→T, and the freed room on E→T takes a new trip O→C→E→T.

No Augmenting Path Is Left

Fan out from O along arcs with positive residual capacity:

  • O→A (1), O→C (1), C→E (1), E→B (4), B→C (2)
  • From A, B, C, E, every arc into D or T is full: A→D 3/3, B→D 4/4, E→D 1/1, E→T 6/6
  • D and T cannot be reached: 14 is optimal

The nodes reached, O, A, B, C, E, are one side of a cut; the arcs from them to D and T are all full. That is the next slide’s theorem at work.

Maximum Flow, Minimum Cut

Cut

Split the nodes into a set with the source and a set with the sink. The cut value is the total capacity of the arcs from the first set to the second.

  • Cut \({\{O, A, B, C, E\} \mid \{D, T\}}\): A→D, B→D, E→D, E→T, value \({3 + 4 + 1 + 6 = 14}\)
  • Every trip from O to T crosses every cut, so any cut value bounds any flow

Max-flow min-cut theorem (Ford and Fulkerson, 1956)

The maximum flow equals the minimum cut value. This is weak and strong duality from lecture 04: the minimum cut problem is the dual of the maximum flow LP.

The minimum cut is unique here (all 32 cuts enumerated; the next are 15). Use: the cut names the bottleneck. To carry more than 14 trips, the park must add capacity on A→D, B→D, E→D or E→T; more capacity anywhere else adds nothing.

Maximum Flow as an LP

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \max~ & \rlap{F} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{Oj} - \sum_j x_{jO} & \quad & {}= F \\ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} & \quad & {}= 0 && \qquad i = A, \dots, E \\ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{Tj} - \sum_j x_{jT} & \quad & {}= -F \\ & x_{ij} & \quad & {}\le u_{ij} && \qquad \text{every arc} \\ & x_{ij} & \quad & {}\ge 0 && \qquad \text{every arc} \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({u_{ij}}\): capacity of arc \({i \to j}\)
  • gurobipy: \({F = 14}\)
  • Augmenting paths solve it by hand; the simplex method solves it too

gurobipy returns another optimal flow of 14 (B→E 3, C→E 4, O→C 4): the maximum flow is unique, the flow pattern is not.

Minimum Cost Flow and Its Special Cases

The Minimum Cost Flow Problem

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{\textstyle\sum_{(i,j)} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & \textstyle\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} & \quad & {}= b_i && \qquad \text{every node } i \\ & x_{ij} & \quad & {}\le u_{ij} && \qquad \text{every arc} \\ & x_{ij} & \quad & {}\ge 0 && \qquad \text{every arc} \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({c_{ij}}\): cost per unit; \({u_{ij}}\): capacity
  • \({b_i}\): net supply; positive at supply nodes, negative at demand nodes
  • One row per node: out minus in

Feasibility needs balance

\({\sum_i b_i = 0}\): the balance rows add up to 0 on the left. Extra supply goes to a dummy demand node.

Integer Flows for Free

Integer solutions property

If every \({b_i}\) and \({u_{ij}}\) is an integer, every basic feasible solution is integer: Solver returns integer flows with no integer constraint.

Why. The basic arcs form a spanning tree, and flows on a tree follow one leaf at a time by adding and subtracting. Distribution Unlimited, DC→W2 at its capacity of 80:

  • Leaf F2: \({x_{F2,DC} = 40}\). W2: \({x_{W2,W1} = 80 - 60 = 20}\)
  • W1: \({x_{F1,W1} = 30 - 20 = 10}\). DC: \({x_{F1,DC} = 80 - 40 = 40}\)

Five Special Cases

Each is a minimum cost flow, so each has integer optimal solutions
Special case Net supplies Arcs
Transportation Sources +, destinations − Source → destination
Assignment Person +1, task −1 Person → task
Transshipment Middle nodes 0 No capacities
Shortest path Origin +1, destination −1 Lengths as costs
Maximum flow All 0 Add T→O at cost −1

The student-to-paper assignment of September 22 was one of these. The network simplex method solves all five, usually much faster than the general simplex method.

Max flow as a min cost flow: the arc T→O with cost -1 and no capacity turns the flow into a circulation, and minimizing -x_TO maximizes it. The notebook solves Seervada’s shortest path and maximum flow this way.

Where Minimum Cost Flows Appear

Application Supply nodes Transshipment nodes Demand nodes
Distribution Factories Warehouses Customers
Food aid (WFP) Suppliers Ports, warehouses Beneficiaries
Solid waste Waste sources Processing plants Landfills
Supply Vendors Warehouses Plants
Cash flow Cash in, by date Short-term investments Cash out, by date

A Minimum Cost Flow Model: Distribution Unlimited

The Network

  • Factories F1 and F2 make 50 and 40 units
  • Warehouses W1 and W2 need 30 and 60
  • Seven lanes, a cost per unit on each; F1→F2 carries at most 10 and DC→W2 at most 80
  • Decide how much to ship on each lane, at least total cost

The Model

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{200x_{F1,F2} + 400x_{F1,DC} + 900x_{F1,W1} + 300x_{F2,DC}} \\ & \rlap{{} + 100x_{DC,W2} + 300x_{W1,W2} + 200x_{W2,W1}} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & x_{F1,F2} + x_{F1,DC} + x_{F1,W1} & \quad & {}= 50 && \qquad \text{F1} \\ & x_{F2,DC} - x_{F1,F2} & \quad & {}= 40 && \qquad \text{F2} \\ & x_{DC,W2} - x_{F1,DC} - x_{F2,DC} & \quad & {}= 0 && \qquad \text{DC} \\ & x_{W1,W2} - x_{F1,W1} - x_{W2,W1} & \quad & {}= -30 && \qquad \text{W1} \\ & x_{W2,W1} - x_{DC,W2} - x_{W1,W2} & \quad & {}= -60 && \qquad \text{W2} \\ & x_{F1,F2} & \quad & {}\le 10 \\ & x_{DC,W2} & \quad & {}\le 80 \\ & x & \quad & {}\ge 0 \end{alignat*} \]

Out minus in on every row: the warehouses’ right-hand sides are negative. Writing a demand row as in minus out = 30 is the same constraint; mixing the two conventions across rows is the classic error.

The Optimal Shipments

  • DC→W2 runs at capacity: W2 keeps 60 and passes 20 on to W1
  • W1 gets its other 10 straight from F1, the $900 lane
  • F1→F2 and W1→W2 stay empty

\[ 900 \cdot 10 + 400 \cdot 40 + 300 \cdot 40 + 100 \cdot 80 + 200 \cdot 20 = \$49{,}000 \]

Node Prices

\({p_i}\): the dual value of node \({i}\)’s balance row (gurobipy).

Node F1 F2 DC W1 W2
\({p_i}\) ($) 900 800 500 0 200
  • One more unit from F1 to W1 costs \({p_{F1} - p_{W1} = 900}\)
  • Reduced cost of a lane: \({c_{ij} - (p_i - p_j)}\)
    • F1→F2: \({200 - (900 - 800) = 100}\), unused
    • W1→W2: \({300 - (0 - 200) = 500}\), unused
    • DC→W2: \({100 - (500 - 200) = -200}\): a unit of capacity saves $200

Every used lane below capacity has reduced cost 0: F1→W1 900 - 900, F1→DC 400 - 400, F2→DC 300 - 300, W2→W1 200 - 200. The prices are defined up to a constant; only differences matter. The capacity of DC→W2 is worth 200 a unit up to 90 units (re-solved at 90: 47,000).

Try It: How Sure Are the Costs?

Download Distribution_Unlimited.xlsx and open it

The unit costs are estimates. Re-solve and ask Solver for the Sensitivity Report.

  1. For each lane, over what range of its cost does the plan stay optimal?
  2. Which cost has the smallest margin for error?
  3. What do the ranges tell management about where to check the estimates first?

gurobipy, confirmed by re-solving: F1-W1 [700, inf), F1-DC (-inf, 500], F1-F2 [100, inf), F2-DC [200, inf), DC-W2 (-inf, 300], W1-W2 [-200, inf), W2-W1 [-300, 400]. Smallest margin, 100, on three lanes: F1→DC up, F1→F2 down, F2→DC down. All three guard the same alternative: past them, 10 units go F1→F2→DC (cost 200 + 300 = 500 against 400 direct). Past the F1-W1, DC-W2 or W2-W1 limits, F1 sends all 30 straight to W1 instead. Ranges hold one cost at a time (checked by re-solving).

Project Scheduling as an LP (Optional)

Reliable Construction

A contractor must build a plant in 40 weeks or less to earn a bonus. Fourteen activities, from excavation (A) to the interior fixtures (N):

Activity A B C D E F G H I J K L M N
Weeks 2 4 10 6 4 5 7 9 7 8 4 5 2 6
After none A B C C E D E, G C F, I J J H K, L
  • “After”: the activities that must finish first
  • How soon can the plant be done, and which activities set that date?

A excavate, B foundation, C rough wall, D roof, E exterior plumbing, F interior plumbing, G exterior siding, H exterior painting, I electrical work, J wallboard, K flooring, L interior painting, M exterior fixtures, N interior fixtures (the 2025 deck, slide 37).

The Project Network

  • Each activity is a node, with its weeks above it; an arc means “must finish before”
  • Critical path: the longest path, A B C E F J L N, \({2 + 4 + 10 + 4 + 5 + 8 + 5 + 6 = 44}\) weeks

Earliest Start Times, by Hand

Activity Earliest start (weeks) Activity Earliest start (weeks)
A 0 H max(E: 16 + 4, G: 22 + 7) = 29
B A: 0 + 2 = 2 I C: 6 + 10 = 16
C B: 2 + 4 = 6 J max(F: 20 + 5, I: 16 + 7) = 25
D C: 6 + 10 = 16 K J: 25 + 8 = 33
E C: 6 + 10 = 16 L J: 25 + 8 = 33
F E: 16 + 4 = 20 M H: 29 + 9 = 38
G D: 16 + 6 = 22 N max(K: 33 + 4, L: 33 + 5) = 38
Finish max(M: 38 + 2, N: 38 + 6) = 44
  • An activity starts when all its predecessors finish: the max of their finish times
  • 44 weeks against a 40-week deadline: the project must be sped up

Two LPs for the Schedule

Earliest finish. \({s_j}\): start of \({j}\); \({d_j}\): its weeks; \({i \to j}\): \({i}\) first.

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{T} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & s_j & \quad & {}\ge s_i + d_i && \qquad i \to j \\ & T & \quad & {}\ge s_j + d_j && \qquad \text{every } j \\ & s & \quad & {}\ge 0 \end{alignat*} \]

gurobipy: \({T = 44}\).

Time-cost trade-off (Kelley, 1961). \({y_j}\): weeks cut from \({j}\), at \({k_j}\) dollars per week, at most \({R_j}\).

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{\textstyle\sum_j k_j\, y_j} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & s_j & \quad & {}\ge s_i + d_i - y_i && \qquad i \to j \\ & s_j + d_j - y_j & \quad & {}\le 40 && \qquad \text{every } j \\ & y_j & \quad & {}\le R_j && \qquad \text{every } j \\ & s, y & \quad & {}\ge 0 \end{alignat*} \]

The dual of the earliest-finish LP is the longest path problem, a flow of one unit from Start to Finish (gurobipy: 44 on A B C E F J L N). The crash costs k_j and limits R_j come from the contractor’s estimates; the course files do not include the textbook’s table, so no numbers are set.

AI Check: Verifying a Minimum Cost Flow Model

Your Turn: Ask, Then Verify

In class

  1. Paste the Distribution Unlimited problem, as on these slides, into an AI assistant. Ask for the LP and gurobipy code that solves it
  2. Before running anything, read the balance constraints: is every row out minus in, and do the signs of the right-hand sides match? Are both capacities there?
  3. Run it in Colab (start with %pip install gurobipy). Does it return $49,000 and DC→W2 at 80? If not, find the error

Course policy

Cite any AI use with the full exchange: date, tool, prompt, reply.

One Exchange, Checked

Claude Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-06. Key lines of the code it returned:

supply = {"F1": 50, "F2": 40, "DC": 0, "W1": -30, "W2": -60}
arcs = {("F1", "F2"): (200, 10), ("DC", "W2"): (100, 80), ...}
x = m.addVars(list(arcs), lb=0, ub={a: arcs[a][1] for a in arcs})
m.addConstr(outflow - inflow == supply[n])   # every node n
  • It stated $49,000 and said it had not run the code; it backed the claim with node prices worked by hand

Verified

Out minus in on every row, demands negative, both capacities present. Run unchanged, it returns $49,000 with DC→W2 at 80: correct.

The Error to Look For

Suppose the code forgets the capacity of DC→W2.

  • Predict. Which lanes change? Does the cost go up or down?
  • DC→W2 is the cheap lane into the warehouses, so it carries all 90 units
  • W1’s 30 units then go around through W2, and F1→W1 is no longer used

What the solver returns

$47,000, $2,000 below the true optimum, for a plan with 90 units on a lane that carries 80. A cheaper answer is the sign of a missing constraint.

Two sign errors, checked with gurobipy. The DC row written as in minus out changes nothing, because its right-hand side is 0. W1’s row written as out minus in = +30 makes the model infeasible: the rows then add up to 60 instead of 0. Full log in modeling-examples/min_cost_flow/ask_then_verify_2026-11-06.md.

Lane P1→H P2→H P1→C1 H→C1 H→C2 P2→C2
Cost ($) 2 3 6 2 4 5

The hub H passes units through; H→C1 carries at most 20.

Practice: Which Special Case?

Practice Problem

For each problem, give the net supply \({b_i}\) of every node and the arcs’ costs and capacities that make it a minimum cost flow:

(a) The shortest path from O to T in Seervada Park.

(b) The maximum number of tram trips per day from O to T.

(c) Three students are matched to three papers, one each, to maximize the total preference score.

(d) Why can the solution of (c) be found without integer constraints?

Conclusions

Summary of Part I

Core takeaways

  • Solved nodes: nearest first; the table records total distance and last connection
  • Shortest path LP: send one unit
  • Spanning tree: add the shortest link to an unconnected node

Watch out for

  • Ties: solve both, keep both last connections
  • Lengths must be nonnegative
  • Greedy works for the tree and fails for the path

Summary of Part II

Core takeaways

  • Augment until no path has room
  • Max flow = min cut
  • Out minus in = \({b_i}\); integer data, integer flows

Watch out for

  • Reverse arcs cancel flow
  • One sign rule for every row
  • A missing capacity looks cheaper

Bottom line

Draw the network first; the model follows from the picture.
